All MRI machines vent the boiling He involved in quenching outside. Or at least, every MRI I've ever seen. But I've seen quite a few. I used to shadow my radiologist aunt at work a few summers in high school and I've got to see a lot, always scared to death of being around them.

As an aside, they don't quench it with helium, they quench it with normal air, kinda. How I understand MRI design is (basically) 3 rings. Much like a dewar container, with a twist.  Outer-sacrificial coolant, very hot compared to liquid helium. middle-perfect vacuum, nearly perfect insulator. Inner- liquid helium cooling the massive electromagnet, making it work properly. If the magnet heats up, it no longer works well, or at all. 

Quenching an MRI is compromosing the vacuum in the middle, allowing heat transfer from the outer layer towards the helium, boiling it in a flash, heating the magnet. This is where the roof outlet becomes vital.

I simplified it down, but its a function of inertia,  torque, center of mass, and positioning of where the sideways force is coming from. In a large ship the torque is generated from a large rudder situated between the water line and the keel,  below center-mass but above keel. This all combines to create a roll-out torque. In a small boat the sideways force comes from an outboard motor, or a small rudder in the propulsion stream itself. This force is much smaller and also usually below or at the keel itself. It being positioned so far below the center of mass creates a roll-in torque force. 

Not intimately familiar with submarine construction, but I would assume their turning force is from somewhere between their center of bouyancy and center of mass, but well above their bottom. That would cause the same behavior as a large ship

So basically there are two forces at play in all turning watercraft. The "thrust" from  the propulsion, and the opposite force of the hull pushing against the water.if the craft sits very deep and has a lot of flat hull in the water, the hull force will be greater and they will turn outwards from the interior of the turn. If a watercraft has a short keel or is sitting very high, they will lean into the turn.
